Hong Kong MPF in four charts: the payroll deduction, employer funding and contribution cap

Use Hong Kong dollars to separate employee and employer mandatory MPF contributions, read the monthly income boundaries and keep cumulative contributions apart from an account balance.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Hong Kong MPF: separate the employee deduction from employer-funded contributions

Interactive planning lab

Employee mandatory contribution for one full wage periodHK$1,000
Employer mandatory contribution from employer funds for that periodHK$1,000
Relevant income less employee MPF contribution, before other deductionsHK$19,000

Hong Kong dollars (HKD) throughout; no CAD conversion. Public regular-monthly-employee contribution rules checked 25 October 2026: each side 5% subject to the HK$30,000 relevant-income ceiling; the employee owes no mandatory contribution below HK$7,100, while the employer still contributes. This model assumes an employee covered by MPF, full regular monthly wage periods, completed employee contribution holiday and no exemption. Whole-HKD relevant income is selected independently and held constant across the chosen periods. No eligibility determination, partial month, non-monthly pay, casual-worker regime, voluntary contribution, tax, other payroll deduction, investment return, fund fee, existing account balance, payment deadline or credited-account date is calculated. The source’s definition of relevant income must be checked; it is not automatically basic salary or the cash actually received.

The central idea

The employee deduction affects the income left after MPF. The employer pays a separate mandatory amount from its own funds. Both calculations depend on the relevant-income rules and the applicable boundaries.

01

Read the employee deduction and the employer amount separately

For an established regular employee with monthly relevant income of HK$20,000, the example calculates HK$1,000 employee mandatory contribution and HK$1,000 employer mandatory contribution.

The employee amount is deducted from relevant income. The employer amount is funded separately by the employer. Deducting both amounts from the employee’s HK$20,000 would count the employer obligation against the wrong cash source.

The MPFA’s public employee contribution page, last reviewed by the authority on 30 April 2026 and checked here on 25 October 2026, supplies the rules. This page uses independent example incomes and no private payroll, MPF holding or account record.

02

The 5% rate operates with a minimum and a capped income base

For the regular monthly employee scenario covered here, each side generally contributes 5%, subject to the published relevant-income rules. The employee minimum is HK$7,100 a month, while the maximum relevant-income base is HK$30,000 a month.

Below HK$7,100, no employee mandatory contribution is required, while the employer still contributes 5% of relevant income. From HK$7,100 through HK$30,000, the employee and employer each contribute 5%. Above HK$30,000, each mandatory amount is capped at HK$1,500.

The grouped chart shows full monthly scenarios around those boundaries. It does not infer an employee’s eligibility or apply these monthly thresholds to a weekly, daily, partial-month or casual-worker calculation.

03

A boundary can change a deduction abruptly

At HK$7,099 of relevant income, the employee contribution in this established-employee illustration is zero, and the employer contribution is HK$354.95. At HK$7,100, the two mandatory contributions are HK$355 each.

The amount left after only the employee MPF deduction therefore changes from HK$7,099 to HK$6,745 across those two examples. That is a payroll-deduction comparison, not a claim that HK$355 of wealth disappears: the employee contribution goes toward retirement provision.

The chart uses distinct scenarios rather than drawing a smooth line across the employee minimum. Actual pay records also require the correct relevant-income classification, employment period and applicable arrangements. Neither chart value is labelled final take-home pay.

04

Relevant income is not automatically the basic-salary line

MPFA’s definition includes monetary employment payments such as wages, salary, commissions, bonuses and certain allowances. An actual calculation needs the source’s classification of the payment, rather than assuming that basic salary is always the complete relevant-income amount.

The calculator asks the reader to enter an independently verified relevant-income figure. It does not classify an allowance, assess a termination payment or decide whether an employment arrangement is exempt. Whole-HKD inputs keep the examples transparent and do not implement a payroll rounding system.

The waterfall subtracts the employee contribution once. At the default HK$20,000, its endpoint is HK$19,000 before any other deductions. Taxes, other payroll adjustments and when cash is actually paid remain separate questions.

05

A lower effective percentage above the cap does not change the stated rate

At HK$40,000 of monthly relevant income, the employee amount is HK$1,500. Dividing it by HK$40,000 gives an effective employee share of 3.75%. At HK$100,000, the same cap is 1.5% of relevant income.

The rule still applies 5% to a maximum HK$30,000 income base. It does not apply 5% to every dollar above that level. The percentage curve begins at HK$7,100, where employee contributions apply, and retains the separate 5% comparison.

This mandatory cap does not calculate voluntary contributions or define an adequate retirement-saving target. A retirement plan needs its own assessment of goals, other assets, time and risk. An employer-funded mandatory contribution is also a different arrangement from a discretionary employer matching policy.

06

Amounts attributable to wage periods are not the current MPF balance

Holding the example income at HK$20,000 across twelve full monthly wage periods gives HK$12,000 attributable to employee mandatory contributions and HK$12,000 to employer mandatory contributions: HK$24,000 combined.

The stacked bars separate those funding sources. They assume constant relevant income and hold the reviewed rule unchanged for the arithmetic window. They do not assert that future limits will remain unchanged or show exactly when a scheme account is credited.

A real account balance can include earlier money, investment gains or losses, fees and other movements. The cumulative contribution total is therefore not labelled account value, investment return or bank cash available for an immediate bill.

07

New employees and payment dates require their own review

MPFA describes an employee contribution holiday for new employment, while the employer’s contribution period begins from the first day. This model deliberately starts after any employee contribution holiday has ended; it does not calculate the holiday or the first remittance deadline.

The pay-record and remittance information also distinguishes the relevant income, employee and employer contributions, and payment date. Those records help reconcile the payroll deduction with money later credited under the applicable arrangements.

Ownership and access are separate concepts. MPFA states that mandatory contributions vest in the employee once paid into the account. That does not make the employer contribution another salary payment into the employee’s everyday bank account. This article calculates no withdrawal entitlement or accessible cash amount.

08

Connect the payroll figure with the retirement ledger and the cash budget

For a household budget, begin with the income actually paid and the deductions that actually apply. For the retirement record, keep employee-funded and employer-funded contributions visible, then reconcile account values and investment movements separately.

The Hong Kong Civil Service Bureau’s MPF arrangements page also distinguishes employer funding from employee deductions and states its dollar amounts in Hong Kong dollars. It is a government-employment context, rather than a replacement for the MPFA guidance controlling this general regular-employee example.

  1. Confirm that the regular monthly employee rules apply.
  2. Check the relevant-income amount and any contribution holiday or exemption.
  3. Calculate the employee deduction and employer contribution separately.
  4. Match actual payroll and contribution records, including dates.
  5. Keep contributions, investment value and everyday spending cash as distinct measures.

The rules and figures on this page were checked on 25 October 2026. The interactive arithmetic does not synchronize automatically with later MPFA changes.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. HKD throughout. Calculations apply public MPFA regular-monthly-employee rules checked 25 October 2026 to independently selected whole-HKD relevant incomes. They assume full wage periods after the employee contribution holiday, with no exemption or special arrangement. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

Calculations assume established employment after the contribution holiday and determine no exemption, partial-period obligation or remittance deadline.
